items.title: Rationalising legal fees: The AI conundrum for law firms and their clients
items.summary: Indian law firms are already using artificial intelligence (AI) and clients have started asking for their bills to reflect that. At a panel in New Delhi on August 17 , Hyundai Motor India's General Counsel Amitabh Lal Das said that law firms should bill fewer hours once AI lets them finish research faster . Das said he had, in his own experience, been charged research fees disproportionate to the advice produced and that he expected AI adoption to bring down companies' external legal spending generally. The instinct behind cutting the bill because the work got faster is understandable. It is also the wrong place to start. A blanket discount treats every hour of AI-assisted work as equally cheapened, when the truth is closer to what Senior Advocate Chander Uday Singh raised at the same panel: generative tools occasionally invent case law that was never delivered and shape answers around what the questioner wants to hear rather than what the law actually holds, a tendency juniors are least equipped to catch. items.title: What India’s reservation debate tells us about the scarcity of opportunity
items.summary: Follow TNM's WhatsApp channel for news updates and story links. After the recent student movement led by the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) over failures in the examination system, Delhi’s Jantar Mantar has housed another andolan: the Reservation Hatao Andolan. An online campaign that reportedly crossed 5.6 million Instagram followers has brought anti-reservation frustration into public view. Some protesters have said they are not against reservation as such, but believe eligibility should be determined by people’s financial condition. The movement, however, has broadly campaigned for the removal of caste-based reservations. The demand raises a familiar question: who should get a scarce opportunity? But the more important question here is why opportunities have become scarce enough for their allocation to generate such intense group competition. India’s reservation debate is partly a debate about scarcity. When limited jobs, educational seats, and public resources are allocated through socially salient categories, competition can acquire a zero-sum character in which one group’s gain is perceived as another’s loss. "Both the Attorney General for India and the Solicitor General for India shall be actively associated with every policy decision taken by the Bar Council of India," the Court directed. items.title: Ex-finance secretary questions GDP calculation, NDTV anchor insists on govt data ‘sanctity’
items.summary: According to the Government of India earlier this week, India’s economy grew 7.8 percent in the April–June quarter of FY27, comfortably beating the Reserve Bank of India’s more conservative 7 percent estimate. On social media, Prime Minister Narendra Modi was quick to call the numbers proof of the country’s “collective strength”, aiming a pointed remark at “doomsayers” along the way, while also urging people to avoid travelling abroad for leisure, host weddings overseas, and refrain from buying gold. Meanwhile, the Congress pushed back, flagging weak agricultural growth, a sluggish manufacturing sector, job creation and rising debt. Into this contest of narratives, NDTV invited Subhash Chandra Garg, India’s former finance secretary, for an interview with anchor Gaurie Dwivedi. What followed was less a Q&A than a visibly awkward conversation about the veracity of the figures released by the government, with Garg suggesting that real quarterly GDP growth was around 2.6 percent rather than 7.8 percent. items.title: Picked up for speaking Bengali: Inside Bengaluru’s Operation Mukta | TNM Ground Report
items.summary: On August 8, hundreds of migrant workers were picked up from settlements across Bengaluru as part of the Karnataka government’s Operation Mukta, a drive to identify undocumented immigrants. For many Bengali-speaking workers, however, the exercise felt less like verification and more like a detention drive. Workers from West Bengal told TNM that police took them to stations and other facilities, checked their Aadhaar and voter IDs, and in several cases went through their phones, including call logs, messages, photographs, and videos. Some said they were assaulted, while others were separated for further questioning because they had made phone calls to relatives in Bangladesh. One worker, Farooq SK, said police initially told them they would be released within minutes after their documents were checked. Instead, they were taken for biometric verification and kept waiting for hours. Police also checked their phones repeatedly. “Phones have personal matters,” he said. “The police take the phones and go through them.” The operation came after months of growing attention around alleged Bangladeshi illegal immigration in Bengaluru. items.title: Complaint before BCI alleges Rashtriya Raksha University law school in 'flagrant violation' of norms
items.summary: A complaint has been filed before the Bar Council of India (BCI) against the School of National Security and Law (SNSL) at Rashtriya Raksha University (RRU), Gandhinagar. SNSL is approved by BCI's Legal Education Committee and at present features in BCI's list of approved Centres of Legal Education (CLEs) for academic session 2026-27. items.title: Karnataka HC slaps ₹1 lakh costs on man who lodged email complaint with CJI and ED Director against ED officer
items.summary: The Karnataka High Court has imposed costs of ₹1 lakh on a litigant who had marked the Chief Justice of India (CJI) and the Delhi High Court Chief Justice on an email seeking the removal of an Enforcement Directorate (ED) officer from an ongoing investigation [ Fair Vakkayil John Vs Union of India ]. The July 25 email was sent to the ED Director's office, accusing an investigating officer of bias and seeking his recusal from the probe. Copies of the email were forwarded to the CJI, the Delhi High Court Chief Justice, the Finance Minister and the ED's Chief Vigilance Officer. Justice Suraj Govindaraj took note of this while dealing with the litigant's writ petition seeking the High Court's intervention in the same issue. The Court, however, found that the petitioner did not place any material to back up his allegations of bias against the ED's investigating officer.
